**Theorem.** Let $P \triangleleft G$ be a normal $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$. Then $\varphi(P) = P$ for every automorphism $\varphi$ of $G$.

**Proof.**

**Step 1: $\varphi(P)$ is a $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$.**

Since $\varphi$ is an automorphism of $G$, it is in particular an injective homomorphism $G \to G$. The image $\varphi(P)$ is therefore a subgroup of $G$. Because $\varphi$ is injective, restriction to $P$ gives an isomorphism $P \xrightarrow{\,\sim\,} \varphi(P)$, so

$$|\varphi(P)| = |P|.$$

By hypothesis $P$ is a $p$-Sylow subgroup, so $|P| = p^{a}$ where $p^{a}$ is the exact highest power of the prime $p$ dividing $|G|$ (i.e., $p^{a} \mid |G|$ and $p^{a+1} \nmid |G|$). Hence $|\varphi(P)| = p^{a}$, which means $\varphi(P)$ is also a $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$.

**Step 2: A normal $p$-Sylow subgroup is unique.**

By the Sylow theorems, any two $p$-Sylow subgroups of $G$ are conjugate: if $Q$ is any $p$-Sylow subgroup, there exists $g \in G$ with $Q = gPg^{-1}$. But $P \triangleleft G$ means $gPg^{-1} = P$ for every $g \in G$. Therefore every $p$-Sylow subgroup equals $P$; in other words, $P$ is the **unique** $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$.

**Step 3: Conclude $\varphi(P) = P$.**

From Step 1, $\varphi(P)$ is a $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$. From Step 2, $P$ is the only $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$. Therefore

$$\varphi(P) = P. \qquad \blacksquare$$

**Remark.** The argument uses only two ingredients: (i) automorphisms preserve subgroup orders (so they permute the set of $p$-Sylow subgroups), and (ii) normality forces the $p$-Sylow subgroup to be unique. The same reasoning shows more generally that any characteristic subgroup of $G$ is preserved by automorphisms; here we proved that a *normal Sylow subgroup is automatically characteristic*.

### PROOF COMPLETE
